title: I am Joseph (Genesis 45:1–15)
hook: he weeps so loudly Egypt hears; "it was not you that sent me hither, but God"

segments.voice: Yesterday, Judah's plea: the brother who said sell him offered to be a slave so Benjamin could go home. Your line was take me instead. Did you make an offer? Day seventy-four.

Judah finishes speaking, and the room goes quiet. The governor can't hold it anymore. He shouts at his servants: everyone out! Clear the room! The Egyptian guards and attendants file out, and the door closes on eleven frightened Hebrew shepherds and one Egyptian lord. Then he starts crying. Not quietly. The text says he wept so loudly that the Egyptians outside heard it, and word reached Pharaoh's house. The brothers have no idea what's happening. They think they're about to be enslaved. Today: two words that change everything.
screen: `EVERYONE OUT!` → `HE WEEPS SO LOUD EGYPT HEARS.` → `THE BROTHERS DON'T UNDERSTAND.`

segments.voice: Then, in Hebrew, with no interpreter now: "I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?" Ani Yosef. And the brothers can't answer. The text says they were terrified at his presence. The rabbis noticed that silence. One old teacher said: if the brothers couldn't answer Joseph when he spoke one sentence, how will any of us answer on the day we're shown our whole lives? Joseph sees their fear, and says: come near to me, please. And they come near. I am Joseph your brother, whom you sold into Egypt. He says it. He doesn't pretend it didn't happen. And then: don't be grieved, and don't be angry with yourselves. God sent me ahead of you to preserve life. Two years of famine, five more to come, and I'm here to keep you alive. And the line the whole story has been building to: "So now it was not you that sent me hither, but God." What is Joseph doing? Readers disagree, honestly. Some hear real forgiveness: he's found a meaning in his suffering, and he frees his brothers from the weight of it. Others notice that he's reframing it for himself, that he needed this story to survive. And the Torah doesn't say the brothers were off the hook; years later, they're still afraid of him. What the text does show is a man looking back over the pit, the slavery, the prison, and seeing a path. Not a good thing. A road that led somewhere. Then he kisses all his brothers, and weeps on them. "And after that his brethren talked with him." For the first time since the coat.
screen: `I AM JOSEPH.` · `THE BROTHERS CAN'T ANSWER.` · `COME NEAR TO ME.` · `NOT YOU THAT SENT ME, BUT GOD.` · then, large: `AND AFTER THAT HIS BRETHREN TALKED WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reframe one old hurt, gently. Settle, and breathe. Think of something hard that happened to you a while ago. Not your deepest wound; something you've had time with. Ask one question: did it lead anywhere? A strength, a friend, a path you wouldn't have found. You don't have to say it was good, or that anyone was right to do it. Some hurts don't reframe, and that's allowed. Just look for the road. The bell holds the time.
I am Joseph. Ani Yosef. Two words, after twenty-two years, and the brothers finally see who has been standing in front of them.
Your line: it led somewhere. Today, when you remember a hard chapter, look for one thing it taught you or led you to. Day seventy-four.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition reads Joseph's words as a model of forgiveness that names the wrong honestly, and Jewish teachers also stress that forgiving does not require pretending a harm was good.

fork.setup: you're Joseph. your brothers are standing in front of you, terrified and silent, after you've told them who you are. what do you say next?
options: remind them exactly what they did.
leave them alone to think about it.
fork.reveal: "come near to me, I pray you." then he names the sale, and tells them it was not you that sent me here, but God.

original.note: Hebrew: I am Joseph. Yosef means he will add.

trapdoor: what you thought: Joseph forgives his brothers and all is well.
what it means: Joseph names the wrong and sees a road through it. readers still disagree about how much he forgave.
what a scholar hears: Genesis Rabbah 93:10: Abba Kohen Bardela reads the brothers' silence as a picture of the day of judgment.
